rawInput.complaint: A 71-year-old Colombian man underwent uneventful phacoemulsification and in-the-bag intraocular lens implantation in the right eye. Preoperatively, best-corrected visual acuity was 20/100 OD and 20/20 OS, with no other ocular abnormalities or systemic disease. On postoperative day 1, uncorrected visual acuity in the right eye was 20/40, intraocular pressure was 10 mmHg, and slit-lamp examination showed diffuse conjunctival hyperemia, anterior chamber cells, mild Descemet folds, medium keratic precipitates, and a poorly defined intraocular foreign body at 12 o’clock. The cornea was otherwise clear. He was treated with dexamethasone eye drops hourly, ciprofloxacin eye drops four times daily, and dexamethasone–tobramycin ointment at bedtime. One week later, visual acuity improved to 20/25, and inflammation decreased to 1+ cells. Ciprofloxacin was stopped at two weeks, steroids were tapered over one month, and ointment continued for one month. Each time steroids were tapered, inflammation recurred and improved upon restarting therapy. Removal of the foreign body was recommended but declined by the patient due to good vision and minimal symptoms. Over six months, topical steroids were modulated to control the inflammation. Nongranulomatous anterior uveitis was considered the leading diagnosis. Erythrocyte sedimentation rate was 24 mm/h; C-reactive protein and antinuclear antibodies were within normal limits, and rheumatologic diseases were excluded on laboratory and physical evaluation. At six months after surgery, further evaluation of the anterior chamber foreign body was planned with gonioscopy.

cotDiagnosis.reasoning:
The chief issue is persistent/recurrent postoperative inflammation in the right eye after otherwise uneventful cataract surgery, with a visible anterior chamber foreign body noted on postoperative day 1. The patient’s practical concern appears to be that vision remained relatively good and symptoms were minimal, which is why he declined removal, but clinically the important problem is inflammation that repeatedly recurs when topical steroids are tapered.

Salient positive findings are: uncomplicated phacoemulsification with in-the-bag IOL implantation; on postoperative day 1, diffuse conjunctival hyperemia, anterior chamber cells, mild Descemet folds, medium keratic precipitates, and a poorly defined intraocular foreign body at 12 o’clock; cornea otherwise clear; IOP 10 mmHg; vision improved from 20/40 on day 1 to 20/25 at one week; inflammation decreased with intensive topical dexamethasone, then repeatedly recurred whenever steroids were tapered over the following 6 months; improvement occurred again when steroids were restarted. Laboratory workup for systemic inflammatory/rheumatologic disease was unrevealing aside from mildly elevated ESR, with normal CRP and ANA, and rheumatologic disease excluded clinically.

Pertinent negatives help narrow the diagnosis. There is no mention of severe pain, hypopyon, marked vision loss, vitritis, corneal infiltrate, wound leak, or progressive deterioration that would strongly suggest acute postoperative infectious endophthalmitis. The cornea was otherwise clear, and vision improved rather than worsened. There is also no evidence supporting a systemic autoimmune uveitis syndrome: no prior ocular inflammation, no systemic disease, and negative rheumatologic evaluation. Although postoperative nongranulomatous anterior uveitis is possible, the striking finding is the visible intraocular foreign body present from day 1 and the steroid-dependent recurrence pattern.

Candidate differentials:
1. Retained intraocular foreign material after cataract surgery causing chronic postoperative anterior uveitis fits best. The foreign body was directly seen at 12 o’clock in the anterior chamber, inflammation began immediately after surgery, and it persisted/recurred whenever steroids were tapered. This pattern strongly supports a mechanical or toxic inflammatory nidus such as retained lens fragment or retained surgical material.
2. Idiopathic/persistent postoperative nongranulomatous anterior uveitis is plausible because the inflammation was anterior, steroid-responsive, and systemic workup was negative. However, this does not explain the observed intraocular foreign body, which provides a more specific local cause.
3. Delayed-onset postoperative endophthalmitis is less likely. Chronic low-grade inflammation after surgery can occur, but this case lacks classic clues such as worsening vision, pain, vitritis, plaque on the capsule, or poor steroid response. Instead, vision remained good and inflammation improved substantially with steroids.
4. Retained lens material is another specific postoperative cause of recurrent inflammation. It could present as an anterior chamber fragment and cause recurrent uveitis. This is closely related to the leading diagnosis of retained intraocular foreign material; however, the case describes a poorly defined foreign body rather than clearly identified lens matter, so the broader retained foreign body explanation is safer.

Narrowing to the single most likely diagnosis: the most compelling feature is the visible anterior chamber foreign body noted immediately after surgery, coupled with chronic steroid-dependent recurrent anterior chamber inflammation over 6 months and exclusion of systemic inflammatory causes. Therefore the most likely diagnosis is chronic postoperative anterior uveitis secondary to a retained intraocular foreign body, most likely retained surgical material in the anterior chamber.

differentialDiagnoses.condition: Chronic postoperative anterior uveitis due to retained intraocular foreign body
differentialDiagnoses.supportingEvidence: Poorly defined anterior chamber foreign body seen at 12 o’clock on postoperative day 1; recurrent anterior chamber inflammation each time steroids were tapered; improvement with restarting steroids; no systemic cause identified.
Anterior chamber cells and keratic precipitates after cataract surgery with steroid responsiveness and negative rheumatologic workup, but less convincing because a foreign body was directly observed.

Postoperative recurrent inflammation is compatible in principle, but vision improved to 20/25, symptoms were minimal, cornea remained clear, and there is no mention of pain, vitritis, hypopyon, or progressive visual decline.
Can cause recurrent postoperative anterior uveitis and may appear as intraocular material, but the case describes an undefined foreign body rather than confirmed lens matter.

cotDiagnosis.finalDiagnosis: Chronic postoperative anterior uveitis secondary to a retained intraocular foreign body
